From the time of the Buddha until the present Śākyamuni World-Honored One, with the exception of the *Avataṃsaka* which directly expounds the Sudden teaching, [the teachings] begin with the Deer Park where the Small Vehicle was bestowed, and proceed until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all of which constitute gradual stages of reception. Thus, the four precepts are either gradual or perfect;
in the Perfect, the four precepts are all perfect, serving as a prologue to the One Vehicle. Whether Perfect or Gradual, none can escape these four stages of progressive advancement.

Furthermore, it must be understood that the perfect does not obstruct the sequential, nor does the sequential obstruct the perfect. According to the Buddha’s intention, the beginning and the end reside in the perfect;
however, because the capacities and conditions [of sentient beings] were not yet fully matured, he employed the three precepts alternately as skillful means to lead them back to the Mahāyāna.

This is why our school establishes the practice from the very outset by first causing one to give rise to a mind of great compassion; the intent lies herein. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Toward..."

If one does not take *maitrī* (loving-kindness) as the object of focus, how could it be permitted that the Great Meaning remains for later? This is the intention of the Buddha, and the Sūtra follows it accordingly;

such is the natural progression of practice—how could there be room for other interpretations? In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the revelation (*vivaraṇa*) and manifestation (*prakāśana*) specifically concern those Śrāvakas of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) and those who had regressed from the Mahāyāna.

Since the responsibility for their assurance is grave, they find it difficult to enter the Mahāyāna immediately; thus, the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*) provide a mediating adjustment until this point where they may finally be revealed.

In terms of its meaning, it is said that through the three cycles [of teaching], the provisional is opened up and the real is revealed, so as to cause those of the three vehicles to collectively enter the One Vehicle.
How could it be that only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is what we rely upon today? The *Śīla-sūtra* is what we set aside today. The Master [Zhiyi] himself stated:

"The four grave prohibitions of the *Śīla-sūtra* are precisely the section on gradual reception from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*" (text). Regarding the term "Péng," this refers to the question: in which text does our school’s setting aside of the *Śīla-sūtra* occur?

If one relies on the passages from the *Fanwang jing* cited by Jie—which denounce the Two Vehicles as heterodox views—and the *Shanji* which describes the Small Vehicle teachings as skillful means (*upāya*), these are precisely the scriptural authorities for the present school’s intention in establishing the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Therefore, when comparing the two categories of precepts regarding the sudden and gradual vehicles:
those received by gradual practitioners are all "gradual," while those received by perfect practitioners are all "perfect"; they differ only in their relationship to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Because *nirvāṇa* is purely perfect and uniquely wondrous, with the great and the small mutually interfusing, [the author] cites two sūtras as the basis for the present Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).

By employing the Great to receive the Small, it serves as the foundation; how could this ever discard those [other teachings]? Right and wrong do not go beyond this single vehicle of wondrous precepts that saves all conditions.
Thus it is known that the Tathāgata possesses only the single vehicle of the perfectly ultimate and wondrous precepts; the *Avataṃsaka* arose directly, while the Deer Park [teachings] were [adapted].

This principle applies throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions; there is no exception to it. According to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*) is precisely this:
it is the opening and revealing for the sake of those great śrāvakas of gradual capacity who have come from the Deer Park. How could they not be of gradual capacity?

It is simply because prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, it had never been explicitly taught that śrāvakas attain Buddhahood; thus, there was a departure from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) which points the small toward the great.
From the perspective of its meaning, the virtuous precepts are excluded as not being the basis for what is currently under discussion;

how could this possibly be a deliberate rejection of the Tiantai school’s own claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* is neither gradual nor sudden? Furthermore, it has never been said that one need not receive the full precepts to be a bodhisattva.
Although the sūtra states, "That which you practice is the bodhisattva path," this is intended to provide encouragement, confirmation, and guidance. As the sūtra says, Śāriputra:
In a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas, you shall uphold the True Dharma, fulfill the path practiced by Bodhisattvas, and attain Buddhahood.

[The Buddha] previously explained before the family that the essence of the Dharma is extracted from the Bodhisattva precepts as a small portion to constitute the five, eight, ten, and full precepts; later, having revealed and manifested them, he bestowed them all upon you.

He addressed him, saying: "At what time was this spoken? Furthermore, it is said that killing and stealing have already been prohibited; why then are they not explained again? To whom does this 're-explanation' refer?

The meaning will become clear from the concluding text itself. If, as Pēng says, only the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) constitutes the reception of the full precepts, then even the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* cannot be used [as authority].
How can such groundless and delusory claims be relied upon? (From the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*)
To disparage the Two Vehicles as heterodox views is precisely intended to cause them to enter the Mahāyāna.
Pēng says: "For five or six hundred years, the gates of the teaching were suppressed and blocked; even now, they remain deficient and cold. How could one possibly find relief?
Furthermore, Master Dazhi, who revived the teachings and contemplations, was born during this very interval—who would not submit to him? Once he emerged... [text ends].
The fivefold doctrinal principles of the Complete Teaching (Yuanzong) are clear and evident; sages have not been lacking in their succession, and to this day they remain unobscured.

As the masters of various schools such as Zhuxi and Zhu’an have eloquently discussed its subtleties and mysteries, even rival traditions praise them—how could Penglue dare to mock them lightly by claiming they lack warmth and investigation?
Penglue said, "I do not know if you have ever read the *Karmavācanā* Sūtra? That sūtra establishes the methods for receiving precepts based upon the Vinaya.
To establish what matter does one first cite the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*? To give rise to the mind of compassion and cultivate the resolve for enlightenment—to establish what dharma?

The commentary explains this passage as follows: "Regarding this precept-dharma, which precept is being referred to? Is it difficult to include [it within the formal ordination], or at what time is it included?

These four points are all for the sake of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*); who would not know this? One should examine that distorted view, namely that this "minor reception" is intended to serve as [a preliminary].
Nada thought he had attained his own purpose and persistently raised difficult questions and doubts, as seen in the following passage regarding the *bai-si* (fourfold) formal act of ordination:

"His groundless and perverse arguments have thrown the teachings into chaos. In the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, it is stated that those at the initial stage of the Three Vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma, yet this was not something he understood.

Although he had been fond of learning throughout his life, when it came to the present, he failed to investigate the teachings; he could not distinguish between the *hua-fa* (transformative) and *zhi-fa* (disciplinary) precepts, nor did he understand them clearly."

Those who receive [the precepts] accordingly fail to recognize cause and effect and do not understand that "perfection" (*pūrṇa*) is the essence of principle while "greatness" (*mahā*) is the gateway of teaching;

they instead claim that the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part motion) ceremony is for receiving the "Great" [precepts], thereby confusing the great with the small. In the *Jishi chao*, it is stated that "generating the mind and receiving the precepts" refers precisely to the Bhikṣu precepts received at present.
Furthermore, in the commentary on the *Ji*, it is explained that "constantly contemplating this practice" refers to the Śrāvaka precepts received through the *jñapti-caturtha* ceremony.

Furthermore, one must deeply contemplate the teachings of the school: when has it ever been said that the ultimate reality of the Great Perfect Circle (*mahāpariniṣpanna*) and its manifestations are inherently inseparable?

Failing to recognize this, one treats the *yikṣu-saṃvara* as three distinct clusters (*triskandha*). In the *Ji yuan ji*, the author himself explains this subtle point: even if a transgression occurs for a mere moment, if one distinguishes [the clusters] in such a way, there will be no confusion regarding the supporting conditions.
Moreover, the *Zi chi* asks: "Is that which is now received here itself the three clusters, or is it not the three clusters? If...

If you say they are identical, must one subsequently receive the Bodhisattva precepts again? Furthermore, since the Great and Small [vehicles] would then be confused, how are they to be distinguished?
If you say they are not identical, since the precepts arise from the mind, once this mind has arisen, why would it not be these very precepts?

This is a great error in understanding, yet you simply seek [the answer] yourself; because you do not seek it for yourself, you fall into such misunderstanding. Why not investigate this thoroughly? If you say they are identical...
The following phrases refute the attachment [to a fixed self]; if one were to say they are not so, it would result in delusion and error.

To receive this essence of the vow, one immediately puts it into practice. The causal and resultant aspects of the Mahāyāna, both for one’s own cultivation and for transforming others, involve profound vows and the complete perfection of the essence of karma.

One should constantly contemplate and cultivate these during the course of practice, manifesting the distant aspiration and progressing toward the reception of the Mahāyāna Threefold Basket (Tripiṭaka).
The three gates of liberation for one’s own practice and the transformation of others both ultimately converge;

when the recipient and the transmission become intermingled, this directly constitutes the cause of the Mahāyāna, which is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena.

Since receiving the great practice and the great vehicle is the true cause, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas, enabling them to reach the immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable [eons].
One who practices the bodhisattva path for kalpas shall attain Buddhahood; with these four words of the *jñapticaturtha-karman*, the three clusters (*triskandha*) are perfected.

That which he taught regarding cause and effect is as easily accessible as this. Because one does not recognize these four kinds of dharmas, one is thus inverted from beginning to end and has no refuge.

The fundamental duty of leaving home is to aspire to the fruit by cultivating the cause; though one may practice the "Transformation City" (*nirmāṇa-pura*), the mind must have its essential point in the first step.
Because one makes a vow and arouses the mind, the karma is perfected all at once and becomes non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), thereby forming the seeds of goodness.

However, making such a vow still belongs to the realm of deluded thought; thus, the *Shishi yaoyong chao* states that arousing the mind in this manner is still a view of false attachment. The *Zhidu lun* says:

"The words spoken by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is beginning their training arise from a mind of false attachment. Yet, when the understanding of the mind is wondrous, it can accord with the true principle (*tattva*). Since this principle is all-encompassing and without limit..."

The Dharma does not require all conditions to be fulfilled in order to realize its meaning; thus, the three vows, the three precepts, the three practices, the three liberations, the three Buddhas, and the three virtues reside within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
Whichever single dharma one raises, it is immediately complete with all others. Although there is a sequence in their verbal expression, in principle they are not distinct.
When the mind receives them in this way, the perfect essence is manifested; when the mind maintains them in this way, the perfect practice is accomplished. This is the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
How could the meaning exceed this? That which is able to act thus—namely, that the supreme bodhi of the *Avataṃsaka* is fundamentally pure—is what is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*).
The desire to see the Buddha-nature within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* all shares this same intent. Furthermore, the subsequent text states:

"Therefore, one correctly upholds [the teaching] by universally taking the Dharma-realm as an object; one courageously makes the three vows, overturning the three obstacles of the past through the power of mental karma, thereby forming the seeds."

The Master himself established the precept-body (*śīla-skandha*) to save those who might fear attachment to this perfect meaning by failing to distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles; therefore, he asked:

"Since the teachings have their respective limits, why is this shown? He replied: "It is to establish the 'partially pervasive' (*fen-tong*) meaning of our own school," and so forth, even supporting the intent of the "profoundly pervasive" (*shen-tong*) section as a preliminary introduction for those who receive the Great Vehicle.
The *Chao* (Commentary) describes the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) as being for the purpose of establishing the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*).
This clarifies that the sequence of practice corresponds to the three bodies, with vows and practices supporting one another and mutually reflecting;

the former refers to the aspiration of the mind for what is received later, while the latter refers to the immediate practice of what was cultivated previously—only then does one see that the profound essence of the Perfect Teaching has its origins.
As for the statement by Penglun, who cites my already settled text to raise a challenge: I do not know how Penglun reached such a conclusion, nor do I understand what he means by "having seen."
Regarding the statement that "the *póngxīn* (蓬心) of the *jiǎngxué* (講學) is buried within the *qū* (曲)," the *zǔchéng* (祖乘) states that the burial of the *póngxīn* lies precisely with you.

Why do you attribute this to the *jiǎngxué*? All that the *jiǎngxué* *póngxīn* speaks of consists of devious ingenuity and the arbitrary fabrication of forced interpretations. The *Jì* (記) says: "That which was practiced by former masters. The *Póngxīn* says:
"Since one has already received the *báisì* (白四) *jìè* (羯磨) for entering the Great [Order], how can one discuss 'immediate' [attainment]? The *Shù* (疏) says: "The intent lies in what follows."
If it is not posterior, with respect to whom could it be prior? Thus, there would be no accumulation that could be established and no body that could be confronted.

If you say it is with respect to the fruit, yet there is no cause; or if you say that by marking the small one becomes large, yet there is no "small" to be marked—without small and without large, how can one discuss "immediacy"?
If it were thus, then being immediately a rat would mean that opening [the eyes] is called "not knowing."

That is to say: one constantly contemplates this practice as being a "small practice," which implies it possesses smallness; yet this very [contemplation] constitutes the three aggregates (*triskandha*), which is the "great practice," implying it possesses greatness.
When the small contains the great, contemplation and wondrous practice are perfectly interfused and correspond with the Great.

Only then is the Great truly the meaning of the Patriarchs; how could it allow for arbitrary or false explanations? The Record states: "This refers to the period of prior cultivation," indicating that what follows is below this point.
The text states: "One should know that this is precisely the arousal of the bodhicitta, the cultivation of the practice of great compassion, and the seeking of the unsurpassed fruit;

this is called the true path, and this is the Mahāyāna. One should know that all the hundreds of thousands of skillful means, the immeasurable dharma-gates, and the various provisional establishments used to gradually entice and guide beings do not originate from this. (Note: In the phrase "one should know that this is precisely the Mahāyāna and all these [characters]," the word "this" ultimately refers to what?)
He asked again: "The Tathāgatas of the three periods and the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest birth and proclaim extinction, suddenly opening [the path].

Do they teach that the Three Aggregates (triskandha) and the Three Bodies (trikāya) are identical or distinct? He answered: "The phrasing differs, but the meaning is one. The Three Bodies are precisely the Three Aggregates and the Three Vows.

The Buddha of Mind is without distinction; cause and effect are non-dual. One who can realize this is only then called a possessor of the Perfect Precepts (pariśuddha-śīla). This is the Pāramitā; it is ultimate."

In conclusion, this very [nature] is that which practitioners of the Way know: if one gives rise to this mind or attains this essence, it is the seed of the three Buddhas, as recorded in the aforementioned text.
Whether cause or fruit, whether for one’s own practice or for transforming others, all are the essence of the vow, possessing all these dharmas.

It is like the earth, which possesses peaches and plums; though they have not yet sprouted from the ground, their branches and leaves are already luxuriant. (This still distinguishes between cultivation and nature. As for the "good seeds":
This is precisely the meaning: how can the manifestation of the complete perfection of the activities of the mind be taken as the already-established Three Collections (*tri-skandha*)?
If it were indeed the ultimate Three Collections, it would also have to be the ultimate Three Buddhas, with all immeasurable Dharma-gates manifesting before one.
This is the natural Maitreya and the spontaneous Śākyamuni; why then did the Patriarch [say otherwise]?

In the following text, the title is explained as the "Dharmakāya Buddha. How could it be that the precept-body (śīla-skandha) which has been produced is already considered a perfected cause-and-effect?

Therefore, fearing that this essence might be forgotten, the commentator clarifies its nature by means of its possession and instructs [the practitioner] to constantly reflect upon it. The Master of Records states:

"This practice is the śrāvaka-precepts produced by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and three proclamations). Because one makes a vow and receives them in accordance with the Perfect Principle, this is the *praṇidhāna* (vow)."

The essence is able to encompass all dharmas. In the preceding section on the conditions for generating the precepts, it was said: "This dharma of the precepts is the primary duty of those who have left the household life;

it is not originally intended for those who harbor great [worldly] resolve, as it is difficult for them to contain [it]. There is a profound reason for this. It further states: "If one did not previously rely upon compassion, how could one accommodate the Great Meaning?
The intent lies in what follows. To summarize the essential point: "Now, recognizing the preceding conditions, one ultimately returns to the city of the Mahāyāna, with the mind dwelling therein."

Thus we know that the entirety of the Patriarch’s commentary begins and ends with this principle of establishing the Perfect School (*yuanzong*) based on both formal reception (*shou*) and spontaneous following (*sui*).
This practice is precisely intended to provide the preliminary conditions for receiving the Great [Precepts], so as to fulfill the wondrous Threefold Aggregate (*tripiṭaka*) of precepts.

Yet, those who are utterly unable to grasp the general purport of the Buddha-dharma do nothing more than desire to receive the Great [Precepts] through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* ritual, while neglecting the Four Cardinal Transgressions of the Good Precepts.
When the *poṇgyun* (the *śuklā caturtha-karman*) is concluded, one’s aspirations are fulfilled and one’s expectations are realized;

having reached the ultimate goal of the three clusters (*triskandha*), is this not indeed the place of supreme attainment for the great vows? I venture to ask: at the time of the formal *śuklā caturtha-karman*, is an object-condition (*ālambana*) employed?

If no object-condition is employed, from what would the substance of the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arise? If an object-condition is employed, why does the Patriarch’s commentary state [otherwise]?
If one is currently receiving the Great Patriarch [Dharma] at this very moment, why say that the intention lies in the future?
Now, regarding the vows established upon receiving the precepts: it is not merely for the severing of evil; the precepts thus aroused are not limited to mere discipline (*vinaya*);

and the practices performed are not dedicated solely to a specific purpose. Because the fruit accomplished does not abide in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one becomes capable of realizing this perfect capacity.
The *Shou daochao* states: "The purpose [of this] is to establish the three clusters [of precepts]; is it not the case that one must receive [them] for them to be so?

If this were indeed the case, then as the former Master Guang took the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) entirely as Mahāyāna, Zhiyi’s *Zizhi* refutes this, saying: "If the *Sifen* is a 'Great' [Vehicle], why is it considered 'Small'?
It would follow that the essence and practice of the Brahma Net [precepts] are entirely identical to those of the Bodhisattva and Śrāvaka precepts, with no distinction between them."
It is certain that this is not so; therefore, the meaning of the Patriarch’s words is intended to be accommodated through partial application (*fen-tong*) to deeply support the doctrinal intent.
Furthermore, regarding those whose minds are equal to the "upper grade" (*shang-pin*), does this mean they are entirely [of the Great Vehicle] or is it a case of partial application? The answer is:

it supports the doctrine of our own school through the principle of partial application. Now, Pēng claims that although those of the upper grade receive the Great [Vehicle], even though it is fundamentally a case of partial application, it ultimately remains restricted to the teaching (*jiao-jú*).

If the "perfectly decisive teaching" (*yuanjue jiao*) is established as being "partially pervasive" (*fentong*) regarding the superior grade of receiving the full precepts (*shouju*), why do you say that the mind of receiving the superior grade of the Great Teaching is precisely the meaning of the Perfect (*yuan*)?
Why do you say that although it is fundamentally partially pervasive, one further establishes the "perfectly decisive"?

One must know that the superior grade of perfect reception is precisely intended to reveal the partially pervasive nature of our own school. Thus, the superior grade of the Perfect School is itself partially pervasive; this is the case if it pertains to the Mahāyāna.

The three clusters (triskandha) are fundamentally and originally perfect; why then would they need to be established [as distinct]? It is precisely because this Great [Vehicle] exists within the Small [Vehicle] that it is said to be "partially applicable" (fen-tong).

If one were already able to realize the Great [Vehicle], there would likewise be no need to establish it separately. Thus, Jieyuan says: "Since it has already manifested as partially applicable, why must it be established separately? The answer is:

although the meaning is indeed pervasive of the Great Teaching, its ultimate conclusion resides in the Small; lest it be confused with the universal [Great Vehicle], it must be established separately.

Lì now examines Páng’s statement and finds three points that are untenable: first, it is incorrect to distinguish the "superior grade" (shàngpǐn) as receiving the Perfect [Teaching] (yuánshòu) while receiving the Small [Vehicle] (xiǎo) is not the Great [Vehicle];

second, it is impossible for the superior grade to be both the Perfect and yet divisible; third, since the definitive meaning (zhèngjué yì) is universally applicable, how can one say it is restricted to a specific teaching?

As the *Jì* states, "The teaching ultimately culminates in the Small," so how could this not be clear? Thus we know that the superior grade of the Perfect reception, when expanded, encompasses both the Small and the Great.
When this is rolled up, it states only in the *Sifen shao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya): "I now receive the precepts for the sake of the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*).
What are the characteristics of these three clusters of precepts? The *Yingluo jing* (Garuḍa Sūtra) states: 'The Bodhisattva’s practice is subsumed within the three clusters.

Regarding the restraint of conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), it is the ultimate severance of evil, karmic bonds, and afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), it is the world..."

Because it involves the ultimate cultivation and realization of the mundane and supramundane vehicles of both the Great and Small [vehicles], those who gather sentient beings must ultimately deliver all conscious beings.
If one merely gives rise to the mind through vows without ever relying on the sūtras to receive instruction, this is merely an empty manifestation of understanding and vows;

the Great Precepts will not be accomplished. Regarding the observance and transgression of these precepts, the Sūtra commands that one seek a teacher for a thousand *li*; how could such ease and negligence be permitted? This is currently for ordinary persons.

Now, although one may have attained the fruit of realization, if one's precepts and conduct are still deficient, even if one dwells in single-mindedness, it is essential to progress through successive stages.
As the ancients said: "Understanding may be perfect, but practice is limited; one must cultivate gradually."

Question: Since it is necessary to practice gradually, I fear this may obstruct the meaning of perfection (yuan). Answer: One practices gradually all day long, yet one advances toward perfection all day long.

If these were not inseparable, then even a person of the first stage of perfection would still have forty-one grades of ignorance remaining unbroken; they would still need to sever them gradually—would this not be perfection?
The authentic teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is straightforward and clear, yet when heterodox people explain it, they turn it into a heterodox dharma.

Although the explicit meaning of the aforementioned text clearly reveals that intent, there is a fear that later generations, with their muddled minds and crooked ingenuity, might further misinterpret it through forced exegesis.
Therefore, I shall again cite the *Śāstra* and *Vyākhyā* to provide a further clarification. In the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is first cited:
"In all cases where one wishes to receive the precepts, one must give rise to a mind of compassion toward all objects; thus, one attains the *adhiśīla* (higher morality)."

Question: The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* cited [in your text] belongs to the Sarvāstivāda school; thus, the notion that one generates compassion and receives the precepts simultaneously is merely a partial or provisional interpretation. Answer:
The record states that while other schools occasionally held this view, it was not as explicit as the five meanings found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Now, I am raising this supplementary point because this is the Buddha’s own intent, not merely the intent of his formal teaching. Our World-Honored Buddha did not fail to reveal this.

Question: Since it is now established that one who arouses the superior mind according to the Perfect Teaching must possess the three vows to accomplish the three precepts, why is it said only that "arousing compassion" and so forth constitutes the precept for saving sentient beings?

Answer: The *Ji yuan* (Explanations of the Source) states: "Although the three precepts mutually contain one another, when it comes to their cultivation and observance, they are constantly used for the purpose of gathering and transforming sentient beings;
thus, they spontaneously encompass all [beings], not merely those in the remaining aggregates. As the treatise says:
Regarding the phrase "all who wish to receive the precepts" (*fan yu shou jie*): since it says "all who wish," there is no distinction made between the great and the small vehicles;

it does not refer solely to the *Dharmaguptaka* school, but rather to the primary practice for those of the three vehicles. Furthermore, this is the fundamental duty of the renunciant. The commentators, grasping the essential meaning, explain this in the sub-commentary (*shu*), stating:

"This dharma of the precepts is the fundamental duty of the renunciant; those who have not long harbored the Great Vehicle will certainly find it difficult to accommodate it. There is a profound reason for this. As for "long" (*su*): [text fragment].

That it is difficult for one who does not harbor great meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to contain profound depth has its reasons; this explains the aforementioned precepts and dharmas. According to the treatise, giving rise to compassion is the primary practice of the Three Vehicles;
furthermore, one must not be ignorant of the Dharma. It is also said that if one does not previously take compassion as an object of focus, how could the "great intention" be contained later?
This explains that the fundamental duty of leaving the household life aims toward the far-reaching and great, yet the realization of this intent lies here, like bending a blade of *pōng* grass.
Taking the provisional teachings as a means to explain this Dharma when there is no other choice, he instead rebuked me, saying: "How shallow and superficial is your grasp of the meaning!

As for the *Śīla-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, which are received by the seven classes of followers—if one does not take compassion as the basis, how could the 'great intention' be contained therein?
The point lies in what follows."
The passage from *Péngyúnshū* (蓬雲疏) stating "the family [of practitioners]" is itself a citation used as proof; why wait for *Péng*’s explanation?

Because of the three groups of precepts (tri-skandha-śīla), how could one ever not accept being entrusted with the affairs of other households?

If you say that this very [practice] constitutes the present acceptance of the great *zizhi* (supporting and maintaining), why do you say that it is intended for the distant goal of the Mahāyāna Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*)? How could the phrase "distantly intending" refer to this very thing?
If Penglai is unwilling to accept the Great [Vehicle], how can he, because of his refusal, cause the flourishing practice of the three groups of precepts in other households to be extinguished?
"Is it not that you are merely pushing the matter onto him?
Penglun said, "I must say that to claim one who has not performed the three-aggregate *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is 'pushing it onto another' is a shallow and narrow view.
I replied, "It is profound; it is not shallow or narrow. It is simply because Penglun has never understood the principle of affairs, whereas I am complete in this principle."
Taking these matters as the substance of experience, there is the principle and fact within awakening for the sages, and the principle and fact within delusion for ordinary beings.

Although delusion and awakening differ, the principle and fact are non-dual. Principle means that all phenomena are perfectly interfused; fact means that each is distinct and not confused with another.

When principle does not depart from fact and fact is not separate from principle, such that principle and fact are one and the same, this alone accords with the ultimate *yuanrong* (perfect interfusion) of the Tiantai school.
This clarifies that the two natures of phenomena and principle—those produced by conditions and those ultimately perfected—are one and the same.

Penglun says: "If even under the four *karmavācanās* of the *śuklavidhi* one can give rise to the three clusters of pure precepts (*tripuṇya-skandha*), who would dare to claim this is a deviation? How much more so when explaining it!

If one stumbles over the Great [Vehicle], it causes deficiency within the Small [Vehicle] and a loss of the Perfect. Because Penglun has damaged and destroyed the Patriarchal Vehicle, he is here rebuked for his narrow-mindedness."
The *Bujin-ki* (Record of Non-exhaustion) states: "The preceding [passages] were all from the Small Vehicle;

this is the Mahāyāna, which uses the Great to resolve the Small. Not 'waiting for reception' (*futaiju*) is the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden (*endon*). This single character ['not waiting'] points to the Perfect essence. Because the Great resolves the Small, the Small is itself the Great; thus there are three resolutions.

Because the principle is perfect, one does not wait for reception, which precisely manifests the meaning of the Sudden. If it were permissible to not receive [the teaching], [it would not be the Sudden]."

To say that [the *Sūtra*] does not require the reception of the Great [Precepts] because one has already possessed them beforehand is incorrect. If it were not dependent on the subsequent reception of the Great [Precepts], how could the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] be established?
To claim otherwise while claiming to understand the meaning of the words is merely false arrogance; do not defile the Patriarchal texts so as to avoid the retribution of suffering.

It is very clear that the abandonment of the Great [Vehicle] stems from a lack of awe and restraint, yet to deliberately incite slander and falsehood can truly be called "committing sin where there was no cause."
The *Péngyǐnshū* states: "To establish the ultimate circle while simultaneously expanding both the large and the small is such that it might even provoke laughter.
This passage is half delusion and half deception. The *Lotus Sūtra* opens up the provisional to reveal the real; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* upholds the rules and discusses the eternal.

These represent the final limit and ultimate peak—the pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous. Our Patriarch relied upon these to establish the Perfect School (*Yuánzōng*); this is the perfection of the Perfect.
Is it not the case that employing this Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng) is to propagate the Great [Vehicle], whereas specializing in authority and the precepts is not to propagate the Small [Vehicle]?

The *Śīla-saptaka* is that which is received by the seven classes of followers; the *Bodhisattva-ben-shi-chao* states: "I now receive the precepts in order to fulfill the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*).

Since these are both propagated together, why do you create such a separation? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "If one merely contemplates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet does not bring them to mind within the Bodhisattva-dharma..."

Those who, upon encountering the Buddha-dharma at the initial stage of joy and delight, immediately believe and accept it, contemplate it, and realize it—this is the discernment that attains the Small [Vehicle].
That within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle, neither two nor three—this is the discernment that attains the Great [Vehicle].
O you, I declare the reason for its accomplishment: you shall certainly attain liberation through the Mahāyāna as I await the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"What you practice is the Bodhisattva path; I pray that you will reveal its true meaning. Although this is merely a jest, it contains profound significance.

To refuse to receive the Bodhisattva precepts in accordance with the sūtras is a failure to distinguish the Great [Vehicle]; to claim that the three clusters of pure precepts (*triskandhaka*) can be generated through the *jñapticaturtha-karman* alone is a failure to distinguish the Small [Vehicle].
To arbitrarily identify these intermediate stages as such is all mere frivolous speech (*prapañca*); how can it be fit for serious investigation?"

Zhepeng said: "My ancestors propagated the Vinaya with 'sublime contemplation' (*vipaśyanā*) as its fundamental substance; when they heard of this [teaching], they would surely have been startled—this is not surprising.
Not only would I have been startled upon hearing it, but would the Master of the Record (*Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya-kāra*) not have been startled when he saw this teaching?
If my ancestors had known of it, how could they not have been surprised? All the great patriarchs and all the World-Honored Ones (*Bhagavān*) would likewise have been surprised."
Péng’s words lack impartiality; the Holy Teacher himself said that delusions are difficult to eliminate and must be dispelled through skillful means.

Thus, the Three Studies were established as the fundamental remedy. As the Vinaya states: "In order to harmonize the three poisons and bring them to an end, the training in increased precepts (adhiśīla) was ordained.

It is clear, therefore, that the Three Studies constitute the public vessel of the Buddha-dharma; how could one treat them all as a single path and exclusively recommend the merit of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) alone? As it says in the Sūtras: [text continues].

It is also said that the precepts are the sovereign of the lineage for unsurpassed bodhi; the Master [of the Text] states that all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time collectively revere the Vinaya.

The Preface to the *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "Thus, these sons of the Buddha practice the prohibitive precepts; from the beginning they differ from the heterodox streams, and do not sink into the sea of birth and death.
The Commentary on the *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "Citing the essential principle to clarify that upholding and violating constitute the standard. The Master of the Record says:

Although the schools derived from the Tripiṭaka differ in what they primarily expound, and while their practices may broadly coincide, they each fall within the scope of specific teachings as previously cited.
Nowhere therein is contemplation presented as the foundation of the Vinaya; rather, these various texts merely discuss the breaking of precepts in terms of their relative superiority or inferiority.
This is the sense in which they are not entirely devoid of connection to the *śīla-vinaya*.

Péngyun: The Buddhas of the ten directions all attain realization and witness the fruit; how could their foundation ever transcend this? Furthermore, since the Buddha takes the five aggregates as his body, why would he rely solely on a single contemplation?
Moreover, you say that the merit of the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles—seeking the higher and transforming those below—lies solely herein.

Yet, have the noble practices of the Three Vehicles ever received the precepts, or are they able to bestow them? If the Way were not distinguished by contemplation, it would be no different from the mundane.

Setting aside for a moment the discussion of shallow and deep, why does the *Dàodǐng lúguàn* (The Towered View of the Path Factors) take the precepts as its pillars? The principles of practice are clearly evident;

why rely on the distinctions of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)? Whether merit or wisdom, vehicle or precept, transformation or regulation, Great or Small [Vehicle], all are universal characteristics of the Dharma.

How could they not ultimately converge in cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), where the two proceed together and the absolute and conventional truths operate in tandem? Our Patriarch’s mastery of the subtleties of contemplation and study reached their ultimate perfection here.

It would be appropriate to propagate these two together; why then is there a separate *Vinaya-mūla*? Furthermore, it is said that the current teachings, meditation, and contemplation all conform to the *Huayan* assembly and are all of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Now, if the teaching is already the One Vehicle, what need is there for the fundamental [meditation] and contemplation?

If the "wondrous contemplation" of Zhongnan Mountain is fundamentally the One Vehicle, why wait for the *Huayan* assembly to be called "wondrous"? Thus, the study of the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*) is likewise the original One Vehicle of the Tathāgata.

The *Lotus Sūtra* represents the ultimate perfection of the wondrous precepts; it merely reveals and clarifies them. In the "Chapter on the Precept-Body," the Record-Master [Daoxuan] deeply realized that reality differs from conventional paths.
Although his intention in dismantling the "thicket" and establishing his own system was to overturn the ordinary, he could not thereby harmonize with the Way.

For those practicing contemplation, there must be the method, the substance, the practice, and the characteristics; how could one take this wondrous contemplation as the fundamental basis for the Vinaya? The conventional path says: "To propagate..."
The Vinaya takes the precepts as its foundation and upholding or violating them as its core principle.
Penglun said: "He uses the language of 'nourishing infants' and 'general understanding' to instruct the deaf and blind regarding the precepts so that they may easily believe them. I replied:

"Even if these are indeed words for nourishing infants and general understanding, what can be done about it? Iron-ear (Tieweng) himself did not understand the patriarchal texts, yet he claimed to belong to the Vinaya school."

It is only through upholding and transgressing that the characteristics of upholding and transgressing truly become profound; unless one has accumulated learning, penetrated the subtle, exhausted the obscure, and fully realized the principles, this meaning is difficult to perceive.
Because [some] claim it is easy to understand, they frequently offer false interpretations. Who does not know the meaning of "wondrous contemplation"?
Yet when its essential application is not mastered, it instead turns into deception and delusion.
Zhepeng said: "Whenever I see scholars of our school presenting the various texts of the Patriarchs for contemplation, each has its own distinct interpretation.

Even within the *Wuyi jie* (Fivefold Interpretation), this particular passage was once analyzed; it is precisely what is meant by being entirely deluded regarding the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) while darkly relying upon the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).

To clarify this meaning, one must first establish the meditative object (*ālambana*), which is discussed here according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) in terms of the undertaking and following of the precepts."
One must take the *dharmadhātu* as the measure, yet remain aware that phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*) differ; while they are not divided, one practices contemplation by means of division.
According to principle, the conditions for receiving the precepts do not go beyond the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).

Although phenomena and principle are mutually identical, their functions (*vṛtti*) are not the same, and thus they cannot be treated as a single uniform whole. Therefore, the *Shoujie yiyi chao* states: "Before receiving [the precepts], evil pervades the *dharmadhātu*; now..."

When one wishes to advance toward receiving [the precepts], because wholesome minds arise in response to the reversal of previously encountered evil objects, the cause for the manifestation of the precepts pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, it must be understood that the limits of the precepts in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) encompass prohibitions against the ten karmic paths; even the slightest stirrings in the mental ground are all included within what is to be restrained and ultimately fall under these limitations.

This does not yet involve the gates of contemplation (*guanmen*). This is a general discussion regarding the scope and limits of the Great Teaching. If, however, we speak in terms of the precepts and contemplation:
The Master’s instruction on the basis for the application of the mind is that it is free from fault regarding food, clothing, the four modes of deportment, speech, silence, movement, and stillness;
yet these objects themselves cannot constitute wholesome or unwholesome karmic actions. Rather, it is solely through precepts and contemplation that one acts in reliance upon them.

Speaking in terms of the training in precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*), the myriad phenomena are vast and manifold—what activity is not the observance of the precepts? At every moment of daily life, nothing falls outside of this. Therefore, the Patriarchal Text says:
I have compiled these various chapters and extensively cited the Tripiṭaka, desiring that you maintain them with vigilance and avoid transgression.

Therefore, I have explained them with profound depth and clarity, determining that they are identical to the disciplinary codes of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Looking toward the distant goal of the sublime precepts of the three aggregates (*triskandha-śīla*), I have traced the origin of faults back to the three poisons.
To sever the source of delusion and provide even deeper protection, I have set forth here the contemplations and antidotes elucidated according to the two gates of transformation and regulation.
When viewing the impurity of lust, arouse compassion for those who kill; when encountering theft, maintain contentment; when facing falsehood, contemplate the truth.

For those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence, let these five contemplations be ever present in the mind while dressing, eating, entering the room, and walking, so that no divergent thoughts arise at the critical moment.
Thus, the Vinaya states: "Always with a single-minded mindfulness, remove all hindrances. Those of middling and inferior capacities may practice these as a single unified set.
Observing those above and studying gradually provides the resources for later practice; by remaining free from transgressions, one achieves observance.

Furthermore, when there are heavy karmic obstructions and deep delusions that are difficult to dispel, one must employ mental visualization (*kalpanā*): visualize sexual desire as the mouth of a snake or a mass of fire;
food as a nest of excrement-eating worms; the alms bowl as a blood-smeared hide or hot iron leaves; and drink as pus and blood—there is nothing here that does not serve to dispel delusion.

This refers to being attached to the pure conduct of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); therefore, the commentary instructs that one must constantly reflect so that the mind has a place of refuge.
The merit of this school’s study of the precepts lies precisely here. As for what is called "conceptualization," the Great Master said:
"Even if it is not yet so, through the power of such conceptualization, if the fear of [failing to] attain Buddhahood arises, it can greatly assist the Path and develop right wisdom—is this not so?"

"Maintaining and upholding [the precepts] assists the practice of the precepts. Students of the later period all know that it is merely like a tuft of grass; they have not heard such things as those cited in the various texts.

If one examines them closely, they are all subsumed within the study of the precepts. To falsely claim that the Patriarch [Zhiyi] intended them to be 'wondrous contemplation' (miaoguan) is impossible—how could the maintenance of the precepts be entirely without mental engagement?

If one lies on the ground merely to maintain the prohibitions, how can this constitute either observance or violation? Furthermore, the citation regarding the classification of teachings belongs to the category of mindfulness."

When the wheel of mindfulness is properly applied to the training in precepts (*śīkṣā*), to what does it ultimately lead? Furthermore, it is said that one should "constantly maintain a single-minded mindfulness to remove all hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).

This uses contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to destroy delusions; because the three poisons are not recognized, the term "hindrances" refers generally to both karma and delusion. Thus, it is taught that the observance of precepts accomplishes contemplation.

Now, since the formal conclusion regarding transgressions belongs properly to the category of the precepts, the *Jingye shu* (Commentary on Constant Mindfulness) states that "constant recollection and constant maintenance" constitute the function of non-action (*avijñapti*).
All practices of the precepts are without "action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*), yet these essential characters of the *dharmas* must be upheld by people;

even if one slightly transgresses through a mental formation, it remains uncertain who would be subject to such a regulation. As for what is called the "object of observation," this is also the sphere guarded against by the training in the precepts;
this refers to the objective sphere. The text says: "Observe the arising and ceasing of phenomena. However, if one does not apply observation to this sphere, how can it be established?
In the noble practice, regardless of its scale, one must clearly discern through contemplation; thus the text says:

"To know that there is no self, person, good, or evil nature and characteristics is to contemplate phenomena as mind. The single character "know" (*zhi*) refers to the contemplating wisdom (*guan-zhi*), while the single character "no" (*wu*) refers to the contemplated realm of truth (*di-jing*).

Within the contemplation of consciousness-only (*wei-shi guan*), the contemplating subject is the mind and the contemplated object is the realm; both are brought into accord through rational contemplation (*li-guan*).
Because it is only within the realm of principle (*li*) that wondrous contemplation (*miaoguān*) is truly established, the *Zizhi* states:

"Of the three natures, the first two take emptiness as their principle, while the latter one takes the mind as its principle; phenomena such as self, person, good, and evil all belong to the dharmas to be sublated by true contemplation.
Master Siming says: "One must distinguish between two levels of subject and object, like a vessel and its contents. If one does not employ principle..."
As for that which serves as the object, it is the observing contemplation that must accord with [reality]. How could one possibly forget or obliterate the self, persons, good, and evil?

One merely pursues phenomenal objects; when has one ever realized the principle? You must know that wherever the Patriarchal teachings clarify the locus of contemplation, there are invariably two layers of subject and object.
Yet, because people merely pursue names and words, they are unable to investigate deeply. Therefore, the Treatise says: "The teaching of wisdom and the locus of wisdom."

All are termed *prajñā* because the wisdom of suchness accords with the principle of suchness. Furthermore, when one first arouses the mind to practice through both the contemplation of phenomena (*shi*) and the contemplation of principle (*li*):

if one contemplates a single thought within phenomena, this is the contemplation of principle within phenomena; if one contemplates the principle within this very mind, it is the contemplation of phenomena within principle.
Therefore, Jingxi said: "That which remains unchanging while following conditions is called nature (*xing*)."
"Unchanging yet following conditions" refers to the arising of the mind; Buddhas, their environments, and their retinues—all such objects may be discussed in this manner.

Now, regarding the school of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), whether in its general or specific aspects, one should likewise discuss it based on these two meanings. Briefly distinguishing the precepts and contemplation, the outline is roughly as follows:

to bend the reed and correct the heterodox, yet not fall within the confines of formal rules—where the precepts do not constitute true precepts and contemplation does not constitute true contemplation.

The deluded belong to the Penglai-Pohe school; where else could they be? Throughout his life, the Iron Old Master (Tiěwēng Zōngshī) took it upon himself to look down on those of the same path, composing works under the name of his own "family business" solely to promote his own views.

He believed that by exhausting all principles, he would ensure their wide dissemination, yet little did he know how deeply he was transgressing and obscuring the ancestral teachings. I, [the author], out of a long-standing and sincere desire for the public good, offered admonitions that seemed appropriate.

To know that one is wrong yet still harbor it with suppressed resentment—how can this be known? What is set forth in the writings follows the ancestral teachings exactly; in principle, it is self-evident.

If one does not recognize one's error, what purpose is served in altering the words of others, burying the true meaning, extensively propagating one's own compositions, and constructing elaborate structures to gloss over false and deviant views?
This serves only to further create vessels for deception; therefore, one must skillfully analyze and investigate the ancestral texts.
How can one fail to see that the correct principle is difficult to shift, while private resentment, false views, and great arrogance all erupt simultaneously within this very text?
Thus, that text states: "If one does not employ contemplative practice, it belongs to conditioned precepts and results in the merit of an ordinary person.
It then cites the Patriarchal text: "If one clings to the precepts as the true Path, then the Path is subsumed under the fetter of precepts," and so forth.
"The Way is near; seek it not afar"—one should reflect upon this (as stated in that text). Yet, what aspect of our Patriarch’s teaching on contemplation (*guan*) has not been explained?

Its essence is precisely this intention: to return solely to the *Caturvarga-vinaya*. This is because the Master of the School extensively examined the three capacities [of practitioners] and took the two deviations as a solemn warning;
he encompassed both the provisional and the real, unified names and principles, and compiled this treasury. It is transmitted through the ages with the record: "Profound."

Because he possessed the capacity to encompass even the shallow teachings, he gathered the doctrines of the Sarvāstivāda school alongside others; because the meaning of these teachings possesses the principle of partial penetration, they ultimately converge with the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng).
The Holy Master, having grasped the intent [of the Buddha], established the Perfect School based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras.

Taking the intention of those schools that "support penetration" as a preliminary introduction for receiving and following the Mahāyāna, all who rely upon this and practice accordingly return to the Path of Reality. Therefore, when he composed and disseminated [this work]:
Encompassing the entire Dharma-realm, when rolled up, it resides solely within the One Vinaya: like stars bowing to the North Star, or water flowing toward the East.
If one relies upon this, it supersedes other extensive disciplinary codes; its ultimate source returns to the school of Wondrous Contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā*).

It is as if a guest resembles his host such that the people of the land find it difficult to distinguish them, yet it causes the Tripiṭaka propagated by this single school—both Great and Small, Precepts and Contemplation, Transformation and Regulation—to be unified.
Regarding the conceptual remedies of the two gates and the clarifications of the sagely words of the patriarchs, [those who rely on them] find no point of return;

both the master and the attendant are lost. As for the three types of rational contemplation (*yuanli guan*), since the sutras that follow the Vinaya have already been usurped as the primary texts, where then is the "following of the Vinaya"?

One may well expect that the Iron Monk (Zhiyi) merely conflated the name of "wondrous contemplation" (*miaoguan*) with superficiality, never having applied his mind to actual study. This is what he did.

If the expansion of the precepts is already deficient and the wisdom of understanding is entirely lacking, how can this not be a failure of adornment? Is it not the case that if one relies on the precepts yet accumulates karma through attachment, it will obstruct the Path?
Since the Buddha-dharma first flowed eastward, the various schools and patriarchs have each proclaimed their teachings and established their own lineages according to their respective foundations;
when have they ever intersected in such a way as to manifest such differences, merely seeking to assert themselves and falsely claiming to have deeply investigated the intentions of the patriarchs?

In truth, this is to bury the holy teachings and allow those who come to study them to easily fall into delusion, thereby creating far-reaching harm. Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
whenever one discusses the four propositions, one seeks to achieve a dual excellence. If one is inferior in precepts (*śīla*) yet superior in contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), how can both be attained?

I say that both the practice of precepts and the practice of contemplation are capable of giving rise to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); for concentration arises from precepts, and wisdom is produced from concentration.

Among the patriarchs of the Tripiṭaka, there are none who have not constantly discoursed on this. It is simply because one does not understand that precepts have degrees of superiority and inferiority, and practices have levels of coarseness and subtlety, that they treat all things as uniform.
To attain samādhi, one must necessarily rely on fundamental contemplation (*mūla-vipaśyanā*).

If you wish to infer the arising of contemplation, concentration, and wisdom from within a jar of mere intellectual views, you will only follow the literal words without ever considering actual cultivation; how then could you achieve understanding? You must know that it begins with the initial resolve of the mind.

In the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), all take the sixth consciousness—the mental consciousness—as the starting point for initiating contemplation; how could this then be considered the state of a beginner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) with a deluded mind?
The *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* states that the speech, receiving of precepts, and generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*) of a beginner are also categorized as conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Thus, the *Shishi yaoyong chao* says: "Such a generation of the resolve is still a deluded thought; it is not that the success of the karmic fruit of one's preceptual conduct does not arise."

When first giving rise to the mind of samādhi and prajñā, one cultivates the meditative observation of samādhi and prajñā; "samādhi" has never been translated into Chinese as "tiáozhí" (straightening and adjusting).

One must simply use samādhi to adjust and balance progress: when there is distraction, one stops; when there is dullness, one illuminates. As observation gradually matures, samādhi and prajñā become increasingly clear.

These two dharmas, śamatha and vipaśyanā, are themselves samādhi and prajñā; this is spoken of in terms of the realization of the dharma-body through cultivation, which is precisely what constitutes observation.

To enter the subsequent stages, one must also rely on contemplation to repeatedly arouse meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), entering them in succession. Regarding what is called "dhyāna-concentration," there are many paths:
the mundane *sāsvāda-dhyāna* (flavorless dhyāna) practiced by the various devas, and the mundane *śuddha-dhyāna* (pure dhyāna) practiced by the disciples of the Buddha.

All of these do not go beyond the four *dhyānas* and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Those among the devas who practice them employ the six modes of contemplation (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-bhāvanā*) to cultivate revulsion toward the suffering of the lower realms.

Coarse hindrances are abandoned by striving for the superior and sublime stages above; through the cultivation of the "earth-dwelling" meditations, one gives rise to the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentration), which enables one to dwell in the Yāma heaven and other realms.
By ascending into the void, one attains the first *dhyāna*, thereby escaping the cage of desire and being reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Progressing through successive stages of cultivation up to the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* (the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) is all termed "worldly savoring *dhyāna*" (*sāsvāda-dhyāna*), as it is cultivated and generated within the framework of the sixfold contemplation (*ṣaḍvidha-vipaśyanā*).
If a disciple of the Buddha cultivates the eight stages of mastery (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) with an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it is called mundane pure meditation (*laukika-śuddha-dhyāna*).
As for the supramundane and the ten types of superior mundane meditations, they are all cultivated and manifested sequentially through untainted contemplative wisdom (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā-jñāna*).

Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that "consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) penetrates the four stages of cultivation. Regarding what is called "wisdom," the *Praise of the Three Jewels* (*Tri-ratna-stotra*) says: "There is no division [between them]."

The distinct wisdom of each moment has more than fifty levels of sharpness and dullness; is this not proof that through the sequential cultivation and arousal of contemplative practice, one can give rise to meditative concentration and wisdom? Thus, this faith is not unfounded.

Zhepeng said to me: "Regarding the single section on the Perfect Teaching of our Patriarch that I have propagated, if one relies solely on various texts, it appears that the precepts merely stop karmic action.
Yet, this text describes the precepts while speaking of 'returning to delusion. Because they do not understand this, they claim that the merit of attaining Buddhahood lies only in the precepts.
If I do not speak of the Patriarchal Vehicle, how can its excellence be revealed? Now I shall briefly explain it; do not think I am seeking to appear extraordinary—you should know."
The Complete (Yuan) School speaks of the precepts as being the One Buddha Vehicle;

this wondrous precept of the One Vehicle is in its entirety free from defilement, in its entirety limpid and concentrated, and in its entirety illumination and function—these three aspects are mutually fused, their essence transcending thought and deliberation.

Even upon examining the preceding and following passages, my conjecture is that such is the intent [of those texts]. Yet, when I privately observe that particular section of the text, it is like one awakening from a drunken stupor, or like one recovering from a fit.
The Mad Patriarchs and the Masters of the Records all expounded upon the beginning and end of the wondrous precepts of the Perfect School’s One Vehicle. Yet Penglai constantly says:

"If one does not employ contemplative practice, it belongs to conditioned precepts that merely produce the blessings of an ordinary person. Suddenly, amidst these words, he speaks of the precepts of the Perfect School as being manifold and calls them "wondrous.
